{{Technical|date=October 2022}}

In [[algebraic number theory]] the '''''n''-th power residue symbol''' (for an integer ''n'' > 2) is a generalization of the (quadratic) [[Legendre symbol]] to ''n''-th powers. These symbols are used in the statement and proof of [[cubic reciprocity|cubic]], [[quartic reciprocity|quartic]], [[octic reciprocity|octic]], [[Artin reciprocity|Artin]], [[Eisenstein reciprocity|Eisenstein]], and related higher<ref>[[Quadratic reciprocity]] deals with squares; higher refers to cubes, fourth, and higher powers.</ref> [[reciprocity law]]s.<ref>All the facts in this article are in Lemmermeyer Ch. 4.1 and Ireland & Rosen Ch. 14.2</ref>

==Definition==

''a'' is called as '''''n''th power residue mod ''m''''' when the [[equation]] <math>x^n \equiv a \mod m</math> has solution. We usually require ''a'' [[coprime]] to ''m'', and sometimes we only consider ''n'' [[divisor|dividing]] <math>\lambda(m)</math>, where <math>\lambda</math> is the [[Carmichael lambda function]].

==Names of ''n''th power residues==

* ''n'' = 2: [[Quadratic residue]]
* ''n'' = 3: [[Cubic residue]]
* ''n'' = 4: [[Quartic residue]] (or [[Biquadratic residue]])
* ''n'' = 5: Quintic residue
* ''n'' = 6: Sextic residue
* ''n'' = 7: Septic residue
* ''n'' = 8: [[Octic residue]]
* ''n'' = 9: Nonic residue
* ''n'' = 10: Decic residue

==Background and notation==
Let ''k'' be an [[algebraic number field]] with [[ring of integers]] <math>\mathcal{O}_k</math> that contains a [[root of unity|primitive ''n''-th root of unity]] <math>\zeta_n.</math>

Let <math>\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_k </math> be a [[prime ideal]] and assume that ''n'' and <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> are [[coprime]] (i.e. <math>n \not \in \mathfrak{p}</math>.)

The [[Norm of an ideal|norm]] of <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is defined as the cardinality of the residue class ring (note that since <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is prime the residue class ring is a [[finite field]]):

:<math>\mathrm{N} \mathfrak{p} := |\mathcal{O}_k / \mathfrak{p}|.</math>  

An analogue of Fermat's theorem holds in <math>\mathcal{O}_k.</math> If <math>\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_k - \mathfrak{p},</math> then 
:<math>\alpha^{\mathrm{N} \mathfrak{p} -1}\equiv 1 \bmod{\mathfrak{p}}. </math>

And finally, suppose <math>\mathrm{N} \mathfrak{p} \equiv 1 \bmod{n}.</math>  These facts imply that

:<math>\alpha^{\frac{\mathrm{N} \mathfrak{p} -1}{n}}\equiv \zeta_n^s\bmod{\mathfrak{p} }</math>  

is well-defined and congruent to a unique <math>n</math>-th root of unity <math>\zeta_n^s.</math>

==Definition==
This root of unity is called  the '''''n''-th power residue symbol for''' <math>\mathcal{O}_k,</math> and is denoted by

:<math>\left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{p} }\right)_n= \zeta_n^s \equiv \alpha^{\frac{\mathrm{N} \mathfrak{p} -1}{n}}\bmod{\mathfrak{p}}.</math>

==Properties==
The ''n''-th power symbol has properties completely analogous to those of the classical (quadratic) [[Jacobi symbol]] (<math>\zeta</math> is a fixed primitive <math>n</math>-th root of unity):

:<math>\left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{p} }\right)_n = \begin{cases}
0 & \alpha\in\mathfrak{p}\\
1 & \alpha\not\in\mathfrak{p}\text{ and } \exists \eta \in\mathcal{O}_k : \alpha \equiv \eta^n \bmod{\mathfrak{p}}\\
\zeta  & \alpha\not\in\mathfrak{p}\text{ and there is no such }\eta
\end{cases}</math>

In all cases (zero and nonzero)

:<math>\left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{p}}\right)_n \equiv \alpha^{\frac{\mathrm{N} \mathfrak{p} -1}{n}}\bmod{\mathfrak{p}}. </math>
:<math> \left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{p}}\right)_n \left(\frac{\beta}{\mathfrak{p}}\right)_n = \left(\frac{\alpha\beta}{\mathfrak{p} }\right)_n </math>
:<math>\alpha \equiv\beta\bmod{\mathfrak{p}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad  \left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{p} }\right)_n  = \left(\frac{\beta}{\mathfrak{p} }\right)_n  </math>

All power residue symbols mod ''n'' are [[Dirichlet character]]s mod ''n'', and the ''m''-th power residue symbol only contains the ''m''-th [[roots of unity]], the ''m''-th power residue symbol mod ''n'' exists if and only if ''m'' divides <math>\lambda(n)</math> (the [[Carmichael lambda function]] of ''n'').

==Relation to the Hilbert symbol==
The ''n''-th power residue symbol is related to the [[Hilbert symbol]] <math>(\cdot,\cdot)_{\mathfrak{p}}</math> for the prime <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> by

:<math>\left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{p} }\right)_n = (\pi, \alpha)_{\mathfrak{p}} </math>

in the case <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> coprime to ''n'', where <math>\pi</math> is any [[uniformising element]] for the [[local field]] <math>K_{\mathfrak{p}}</math>.<ref name=Neu336>Neukirch (1999) p. 336</ref>

==Generalizations==
The <math>n</math>-th power symbol may be extended to take non-prime ideals or non-zero elements as its "denominator", in the same way that the [[Jacobi symbol]] extends the Legendre symbol.

Any ideal <math>\mathfrak{a}\subset\mathcal{O}_k</math> is the product of prime ideals, and in one way only:
:<math>\mathfrak{a} = \mathfrak{p}_1 \cdots\mathfrak{p}_g.</math>

The <math>n</math>-th power symbol is extended multiplicatively:

:<math> \left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{p}_1 }\right)_n  \cdots \left(\frac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{p}_g }\right)_n.  </math>

For <math>0 \neq \beta\in\mathcal{O}_k</math> then we define
:<math>\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right)_n := \left(\frac{\alpha}{(\beta) }\right)_n,</math> 

where <math>(\beta)</math> is the principal ideal generated by <math>\beta.</math>

Analogous to the quadratic Jacobi symbol, this symbol is multiplicative in the top and bottom parameters.

* If <math>\alpha\equiv\beta\bmod{\mathfrak{a}}</math> then <math>\left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n = \left(\tfrac{\beta}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n. </math>
*<math> \left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n  \left(\tfrac{\beta}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n  = \left(\tfrac{\alpha\beta}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n.  </math>
* <math> \left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n  \left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{b} }\right)_n = \left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{ab} }\right)_n. </math>

Since the symbol is always an <math>n</math>-th root of unity, because of its multiplicativity it is equal to 1 whenever one parameter is an <math>n</math>-th power; the converse is not true.

* If <math>\alpha\equiv\eta^n\bmod{\mathfrak{a}}</math> then <math>\left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n =1. </math>
* If  <math> \left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n \neq 1</math> then <math>\alpha</math> is not an <math>n</math>-th power modulo <math>\mathfrak{a}.</math>
* If <math> \left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\mathfrak{a} }\right)_n =1</math> then <math>\alpha</math> may or may not be an <math>n</math>-th power modulo <math>\mathfrak{a}.</math>

==Power reciprocity law==
The ''power reciprocity law'', the analogue of the [[law of quadratic reciprocity]], may be formulated in terms of the [[Hilbert symbol]]s as<ref name=Neu415>Neukirch (1999) p. 415</ref>

:<math>\left({\frac{\alpha}{\beta}}\right)_n \left({\frac{\beta}{\alpha}}\right)_n^{-1} = \prod_{\mathfrak{p} | n\infty} (\alpha,\beta)_{\mathfrak{p}},</math>

whenever <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are coprime.
